claims.text: The as-synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalyst has a random atomic distribution.
Controlled post-synthesis annealing can induce slight short-range atomic ordering in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs.
The proposed annealing can induce short-range ordering without causing macroscopic phase separation.
Short-range atomic ordering modifies the local electronic structure of catalyst surface sites.
Short-range ordering shifts the d-band center of PtPdRhRuIrOs surface atoms.
A shift in the d-band center changes the adsorption energies of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The annealing-induced electronic change reduces the adsorption strength of poisoning intermediates.
Reduced adsorption of poisoning intermediates lowers the rate of catalyst poisoning.
A lower poisoning rate improves catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the annealed catalyst will exhibit a measurable d-band-center shift.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the annealed catalyst will exhibit lower surface-poisoning levels.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the annealed catalyst will retain activity longer and degrade more slowly.
The proposed effect should hold during ethanol oxidation in acidic media at fuel-cell-relevant potentials and 60–80 °C.
The proposed effect is limited to treatments that do not cause phase segregation or other drastic structural changes.
Prior d-band theory and studies on simpler systems support a relationship between electronic-structure changes and adsorption energies.
The magnitude and precise impact of the proposed effects in the six-element catalyst are uncertain.
Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy or a similar method can detect the proposed d-band-center shift.
In situ infrared or Raman spectroscopy can quantify the relevant surface-poisoning intermediates.
